title: What Is Private Equity? A Guide to Private Markets

sentences.text: Do you think you're investing in the world's biggest and fastest growing companies through your stock market holdings?
You may be missing out on more than you think.
Nearly 90% of the biggest companies are privately owned, meaning they don't trade on a stock exchange.
For decades, investing in these privately owned businesses was largely reserved for institutions and the ultra wealthy.
Today, that is changing.
We're taking a closer look at private markets, a $13 trillion ecosystem that represents a huge part of the global economy.
So in this video, we're going to break down the four main private market asset classes private equity, private real estate, private credit and private infrastructure.
What they are, how they work and why investors value them.
Now private markets might sound complicated, but the idea behind them is really very simple.
At their core, these are just investments in companies and assets that don't trade on public exchanges.
That can mean businesses, real estate loans or even infrastructure.
They could be the warehouse shipping, your online order or a data center powering your favorite apps.
Once you see that private markets starts to feel a lot less abstract and more like what they actually are an important part of the economy.
Of all the asset classes within private markets, the one you've probably heard most about is private equity.
For decades, it's been a preferred strategy for some of the world's most experienced investors.
They usually have two goals in mind to diversify beyond public stocks and bonds, and to potentially earn better returns than they'd get elsewhere.
Let's walk through it with Viral Patel.
One of my colleagues here at Blackstone and CEO of BXPE.
Okay, so let's start with the basics then.
What is private equity?
It's really not as complicated as sometimes it can seem.
Most people think about investing in companies in the public markets.
Meaning we're buying and trading a stock on the New York Stock Exchange or the Nasdaq.
And in that case, you're just buying a piece of a company in private equity.
What we're doing is we're buying the entire company.
But oftentimes much earlier in that company's journey before a company has gone public where we're partnering with a management team helping it grow its business,
and then figuring out how to exit it.
And oftentimes that's because a founder, a management team, an existing owner, is looking for additional help to figure out ways to grow.
They've kind of taken the business as far as they can, and now they're looking for a partner that can help them get to the next level.
So the concept seems pretty simple.
And yet the industry has attracted a little bit of a noise and attention over the years.
Why do you think that is?
Well, part of it is I think it's an industry that's really growing a lot. Right?
This has been if you went back to the 90s, private equity is more of a cottage industry today.
It's much more mainstream.
There's this misconception that can be out there that private equity is about cost cutting and reduction.
It's really the opposite.
Private equity is about building and growing companies to make them bigger and stronger than they were before we got involved.
Okay, so let's start there.
So how does private equity actually work?
So a lot of it starts with thematic investing right.
Thinking long term about where we're seeing the world going and how do we invest behind those areas.
And then once we've got a theme that we like, we ask our investment teams to really try to canvass the market.
We spend a lot of time trying to understand the answer to a pretty simple question.
How important is this company?
An important company is one where if it were to go away, its customers would have a real issue. Right.
And trying to understand how important that is, how durable its revenues are going to be, how much pricing power does it actually have in the marketplace?
How many competitors are there?
Where is the market going?
So we're spending time understanding that business in the context of the market it sits in.
And then most importantly, what can we do with these businesses. Right.
How can we change them?
How can we help them grow?
And once we've decided that that's really how we can figure out which ones we want to invest behind, sort of a business building plan.
When you go into these investments 100% it's business building.
That's what we're actually looking to do with all of our companies.
So over the lifespan of an investment, you bring in a lot of operational resources to help the company grow.
What sort of resources and expertise do you do you bring?
We look for what do these businesses need.
And we tailor make the resources to make them available for that, that purpose.
So as an example, companies that want to add to their C-suite, whether maybe it's a new technology officer,
a new financial chief financial officer, we have an extensive network as an industry of talent that we can bring into an organization.
We can help with AI implementation.
We can help with thinking through how to navigate geopolitical concerns that are that are occurring.
We can help thinking through where the market and the economies are going to help position our businesses.
And so it's really about matching the wealth of resources that we have at our disposal with what these businesses need in order to help them drive.
So how does a private equity investor decide when it's time to sell?
Well, when we choose to sell, which in industry jargon we call an exit is really a function of the market opportunity at that time.
And I think what we found is if you build a great business and you think long term, the exit almost presents itself at the right moment.
But the key to all of those is really focus on long term value accretion,
because what we want to make sure we're doing is making investments in these companies so they can continue to compete for decades,
not just this year, not short term investments.
So the goal is really leaving them stronger than you found them.
Of course, 100%.
So let's talk about a recent private equity investment made by Blackstone into Jersey Mike's the iconic franchise chain.
So how did that one work out?
So you know, Jersey Mike's long standing franchise, 50 years Peter Cancro had been running that he grew it from one store to 3000 stores.
So already a really substantial business.
But again, Peter was looking to take this business to the next level.
He was looking to transition out of the business and potentially even take it public.
And so we were able to help him prepare the company internally to go public.
We were able to help him recruit a successor.
So we brought in Charlie Morrison, who was the former CEO of Wingstop.
We were able to bring out a new brand ambassador, Eli Manning.
I'm a big Giants fan, so I was very excited to see to see that happen.
A big part of a business like Jersey Mike's is opening new stores, and for us, as one of the largest real estate investors in the world.
This was something that we were able to help them think through at a really crucial moment in their growth journey.
Institutions have been investing in private equity for decades.
Why has it been so attractive for them?
The growth of the private equity industry has historically been fueled by institutions,
and it's interesting that if you if you speak to these institutions,
20 maybe even 30% of their overall portfolios can be in private markets with a substantial amount allocated to private equity.
And what they would tell you is they like the allocation to private equity for really two reasons.
One is diversification.
A lot of investors think about building a diversified equity portfolio with public equities.
But the problem is public equities are only about 10% of the overall global market.
Nearly 90% of companies are actually private.
What's happened is the number of public companies has actually declined over the last 20 years.
You have less companies going public today, and the ones that are going public are waiting longer to go public.
And so the private markets become a really important part of a portfolio because you get access to these companies earlier,
you get to participate in a lot of their growth and their value creation much, much earlier.
The second thing is, at least historically, the private markets have delivered excess returns above public markets.
So how should individual investors think about private equity?
So those benefits are still there for individual investors meaning the benefit of diversification the benefit for increased increased return.
Now it's going to come with the trade off which is this is a less liquid asset class.
However for a portion of your portfolio where you don't need that daily or near-term liquidity, this can be a way of enhancing overall portfolio performance.
I think what's really changed is the access point.
Individual investors now have many more options available to them to enter into private markets,
particularly options that give them a little bit more liquidity into the asset class.
When most people here real estate investing, they picture buying a house or maybe a rental property.
But in private markets, real estate is a massive, diverse asset class that goes way beyond that.
And it's backed by hard, tangible assets.
Here to help us bring this all to life, is A.J.
Agarwal, co-president and director of BREIT.
Tell me what, what is private real estate and how does that differ from, say, an individual buying a home or a small business?
Yeah, it's a great question because oftentimes when I tell people we invest in real estate, they think we're buying houses.
But the reality is we're investing in commercial real estate here.
We're buying assets for investment purposes that are generating income.
And then people ask, well, what's the difference between public real estate and private real estate?
You can invest in real estate publicly by buying publicly traded REITs.
There are quite a few of them that are listed.
Apartment REITs office REITs, shopping center REITs.
Private real estate is just not publicly traded on an exchange like the New York Stock Exchange.
And interestingly, in America, 90% of all commercial real estate is actually privately held outside of the public markets.
So if you don't actually want to include private real estate in your investment portfolio, it's like you're ignoring 90% of the market.
It's almost like if you wanted to write a book and just use three letters of the alphabet A, B,
and C and ignore the other 90% of the letters.
So why is private real estate, which is also sometimes called real assets?
Why is that so attractive right now?
It's helpful to know that real estate is the third largest asset class in America.
After stocks and bonds.
And it's also helpful to know the most sophisticated institutional investors in America and globally,
oftentimes have a double digit waiting to real estate in their investment portfolios, in addition to stocks, in addition to bonds.
And when you had what people call the traditional 60/40 portfolio, 60% weighted to equities, 40% weighted to bonds.
The reason that historically worked is that when stocks would go down, bonds would go up and then vice versa.
Unfortunately, in the last five years, more than 75% of the time when stocks would go down, bonds would go down.
And so you're not getting the portfolio diversification that you really need.
Now why real assets or why real estate.
Well, real assets and real estate can offer real diversification because it's lowly correlated with both stocks and bonds.
And if you look over the last 10 or 20 years,
if you had added, for example, a 20%, 10% allocation of private real estate to a typical 60/40 portfolio,
amazingly, you would have had higher returns, higher income generation and lower volatility.
Because these are income producing assets right?
That's why people want to be in real estate.
They're hard assets generating durable, consistent income.
And that income leads to cash flows growing, which in addition to income generation then also leads to asset appreciation.
So with all the forces that we're seeing right now around artificial intelligence or the migration of our lives online,
where do you where do you want to play that from a real estate perspective?
So it's really important to pick the right real estate sectors.
When I started here at Blackstone, the sexiest, most institutional, highest quality real estate assets would have been office buildings and shopping malls.
And by the way, today you couldn't find two asset sectors that we are less favorable towards.
And so it's very important to think about how people are living, working, shopping, playing,
and think about how that affects what kind of real estate you want to own.
And today, as you pointed out, we're seeing a number of macro trends that are affecting the demand for different real estate asset classes.
For example, not surprisingly, I think most people are ordering more things online.
They're going to Walmart.com, they're going to Amazon.com, they're going to Target.com, whatever it is, they're ordering more things online this year than last year.
It turns out for every extra billion dollars that people are spending online, we need about 1 million more square feet of warehouse space. That's remarkable.
Or streaming media?
More people using social media.
More people using digital photography, more people streaming music.
What does that mean?
Well, they say it.
It means that it's growing the need for the cloud.
But the cloud.
Christine, the cloud is not up there.
It's on the ground in data centers.
So I think it's really important to watch trends, watch how people are living, working, shopping, playing and make sure that what you're buying reflects those trends.
I've heard some people say that buying these sorts of assets is the cheapest way to play AI.
Do you agree?
I think that buying these types of assets is a very attractive way of playing technology trends and AI trends.
If you own a warehouse, you're not betting if targets going to win or Walmart's going to win or Amazon's going,
you're just betting that e-commerce is going to win.
So for financial advisors thinking about their own portfolios, where does real estate fit in?
We think that real estate is a complement to traditional 60/40 portfolios.
We're not advocating that 100% of portfolios should be real estate, but we are advocating that there is a role for asset sectors.
Asset classes, like real estate, that are lowly correlated with the performance of bonds, lowly correlated with the performance of equities.
I just go back to the math that if you backward tested the addition of private real estate to a traditional 60/40 portfolio,
if you added a 10% or 20% allocation of private real estate over the last 10 or 20 years,
you would have actually had a portfolio that was more efficient, that generated higher returns than just that 60/40 portfolio, higher income, all while delivering less volatility.
If private equity is about owning companies and private real estate is about owning buildings, then private credit is about lending money to help us understand why.
I'm joined by my colleague Victoria Chant, global head of capital markets for Blackstone Credit and Insurance.
We want to start foundationally.
Tell us what is private credit.
So private credit is really the business of lending directly to high quality companies and creating customized,
flexible solutions for companies to build and grow their businesses and break it down very simply,
how does private credit work will work with them directly on whatever capital need they're looking to solve,
and will create something flexible and customized that solves that need and in exchange for that, will get paid a coupon,
get paid effectively interest on the loan that we're making on a periodic basis.
Because we're actually negotiating directly with a company, and we're also offering a customized solution to companies.
We're actually getting a higher premium.
What kind of companies are seeking out private credit?
I would say all kinds of companies across the spectrum.
The highest quality companies are generally the ones that we tend to gravitate towards, of course.
But it's companies really oftentimes that are looking for a little bit more flexibility.
And they're looking for that flexibility oftentimes because they're in growth mode, they're looking to figure out how to build.
And they need something a little bit more flexible than what those public markets have traditionally delivered.
I think the reason we've seen so much growth in private credit is really because the need is so large,
it's so much bigger than what the banks can actually solve and fill.
And so when you look across the spectrum of really good quality companies across the country,
we think about the fact that there's no one size fits all for all these companies.
There are different points in their cycle. They're growing.
They're trying to expand.
So I think we're just even still scratching the surface in terms of where we can actually leave supply capital in these markets.
So part of investing in private credit is knowing where to invest in what you call the capital stack, right.
There are various various levels of debt and equity. Right.
So how do you how do you make those decisions?
Well, why don't we talk a little bit about what what does capital stack mean.
So what we mean by that is when I'm lending to a company, what's my ability to get repaid?
Is there anyone else's going to get repaid first in private credit?
We want to be senior.
What I mean by that is we want to be the first one to get repaid on the loan.
We don't want anyone ahead of us in that.
And that's the majority of what is happening in the private credit markets.
So as you and I both know, there's been quite a bit of noise about private credit.
Why is that?
What's your take?
Well, I think part of it is anytime you have a new asset class that's been emerging, you're going to get a lot of questions,
and there's going to be a lot of skepticism over how that's going to perform.
I think if you actually just break down what's happening in private credit, we're lending on a senior secured basis to high quality companies.
So private credit is a relatively new asset class, correct? It is.
Although the business of lending has been around for a very, very long time.
And so the business of lending to high quality companies has been around forever.
We're just doing it in a slightly different way, a little bit more directly than we've seen for some time.
And why is it helpful to have that as part of a diversified portfolio?
I think it's actually great diversified.
It's not something that is going to necessarily track to a portfolio of liquid investments…
that may be at the whim of what's going on in the volatility in the markets.
It's a stable stream of income.
In general, when investing in this asset class, you're really investing in a portfolio of private credit loans.
And so you're getting the benefit of access to a diversified portfolio of income generating investments.
And that can be really attractive to add to a portfolio that's really very much focused on public markets.
It behaves and performs a little bit differently.
And so that's a great non correlated diversifier.
Any key takeaways for viewers about private credit?
I think the most important thing I think about is that private credit is really…
here to say I expect this to be an asset class that is around forever.
It will evolve, of course, over time as it grows and matures.
But we've seen what it can do.
We've seen how effective it can be when the banking market is not available and other markets are not available.
And I think that is going to be something that is tried and true.
Certainly a staggering demand for capital in this day and age.
So absolutely, it's exciting time to be here.
We tend to think of infrastructure as roads, bridges and airports,
but today it's really so much more as the world's demand for these essential systems grow, so does the need for capital.
Let's take a closer look with my colleague Greg Blank, CEO of BXINFRA.
Okay. So I'm curious.
So people must ask you all the time is infrastructure really sort of bridges, roads tunnels.
Is that what is that what we're talking about still today?
That's a portion of it, but only a small portion.
It's really around more of the modern economy.
Think about it as the essential services that drive our lives that we don't really think about.
I've heard you talk about infrastructures really being in three broad categories.
Will you walk me through each of those?
The first digital infrastructure.
What is that?
So digital infrastructure.
I think about this is when you take out your cell phone,
you tap on an application that's using all three elements of digital infrastructure, the software that runs the application.
It's sitting in a data center hundreds of thousands of miles away.
When you tap it, it's being transmitted on a cellular network to a cell phone tower, a mile or two from where you sit.
And then there's a fiber optic cable that sends that data back and forth and thousands of times a day.
It's really powering the modern economy.
And that is what digital infrastructure is.
So the second bucket is energy infrastructure.
So if you think about everything you need to keep the lights on in this room or power your business,
it's an entire series of investments across the energy value chain.
It's investment from pipelines to power plants, natural gas and renewables, transmission lines, investments and utilities to upgrade their systems and networks.
Electricity demand in the country has been flat for the last 40 years.
It's now projected to grow 40 to 50% over the next decade.
All of these are critical to deliver the electrons, to run our economy and keep the lights on all of our homes and businesses.
Okay, then finally, some of the more traditional assets which are in sort of transportation infrastructure,
this is ports, airports, roads, can be marinas, aviation logistics infrastructure to deliver a package to your house.
So everything around those elements that are big, hard assets that require a lot of capital.
So it's everywhere. It's everywhere.
You just don't think about it.
It's not a household name, but it's mission critical.
It's essential to your life.
Tell us a little bit about the massive need for capital and private infrastructure right now.
There's a huge need for capital, whether it's $100 trillion that's some of estimated.
So there's a ton of capital required to build out our energy infrastructure, our transportation logistics and our digital infrastructure.
Our infrastructure is old, whether it's the roads, whether it's utility poles that are 50 years old.
These all require significant upgrades of capital.
A lot of these projects, they do take a long time and that's why it's really important.
They're very capital intensive.
We invest a lot of capital.
We need long term contracts to basically earn an adequate return on investing in these projects.
But because we're powering the modern economy, it's incredibly important to have this long duration and give us the ability to continue investing over time.
And many of these require government partnership as well.
How does that work?
In a lot of these situations the government really identifies the need in private capital fills in the project.
And so as we think about that, whether it's the digitization, whether it's energy, this capital is coming from private sources.
So we work with governmental bodies sometimes regulators, but it's really private capital that's going to fund these projects and fund the next generation of growth.
What makes this really unique for an investor?
So infrastructure has some defining characteristics.
It really comes back to having long term contracted cash flows as you think about it.
When we build a project so we build an energy project, we build a pipeline, we build a power plant.
We have a 20 year contract with the customer to buy all the power from that facility.
What does that mean?
It means low volatility.
So it doesn't go up.
It doesn't go down significantly.
When the economy goes up and down at the same time, it diversifies an investor's portfolio.
This is really, really important.
As you think about asset classes tend to go up and down together.
Infrastructure by nature of its contracts, the sectors we're investing in is way less volatile.
And you saw that through Covid, through the global financial crisis, where returns were very stable even when the economy faltered.
I think this is really the part of your portfolio where you sleep well at night.
Infrastructure continues to perform and gives that diversification exactly when you need it.
Now there are powerful forces changing the world around us, and they're expanding the need for private capital rapidly.
When you zoom out, it's clear the overall investable market is far larger than what's currently being utilized by individual investors.
What's changing now is access.
Individuals have more opportunities than ever before.
The asset classes we've covered private equity, private real estate, private credit, private infrastructure are becoming more and more important to understand.
And as the world continues to change around us,
we believe these private companies and investments are likely to play an even bigger role in shaping what comes next.

ko: 당신은 주식 시장 투자를 통해 세계에서 가장 크고 빠르게 성장하는 기업들에 투자하고 있다고 생각하십니까?
당신은 생각보다 더 많은 것을 놓치고 있을지도 모릅니다.
대기업의 거의 90%는 비상장 기업으로, 주식 시장에 상장되어 있지 않습니다.
수십 년 동안 이러한 비상장 기업에 대한 투자는 주로 기관 투자자와 초고액 자산가들에게만 국한되었습니다.
오늘날, 그 상황이 바뀌고 있습니다.
우리는 세계 경제의 상당 부분을 차지하는 13조 달러 규모의 생태계인 민간 시장을 자세히 살펴보고 있습니다.
이번 영상에서는 사모 시장의 주요 자산 유형 4가지, 즉 사모 펀드, 사모 부동산, 사모 대출, 사모 인프라에 대해 자세히 살펴보겠습니다.
그것들이 무엇이고, 어떻게 작동하며, 투자자들이 왜 그것들을 가치 있게 여기는지 알아보겠습니다.
사모 시장은 복잡해 보일 수 있지만, 그 기본 개념은 사실 매우 간단합니다.
본질적으로 이것들은 공개 거래소에서 거래되지 않는 회사와 자산에 대한 투자일 뿐입니다.
이는 기업, 부동산 대출 또는 인프라를 의미할 수 있습니다.
창고 배송, 온라인 주문 또는 즐겨 사용하는 앱에 전력을 공급하는 데이터 센터일 수 있습니다.
일단 사적 시장이 추상적인 개념에서 벗어나 경제의 중요한 부분이라는 것을 깨닫게 되면, 사적 시장이 훨씬 더 현실적으로 느껴지기 시작할 것입니다.
사모 시장 내 모든 자산 유형 중에서 여러분이 가장 많이 들어봤을 것은 아마도 사모 펀드일 것입니다.
수십 년 동안 이는 세계에서 가장 경험이 풍부한 투자자들이 선호하는 전략이었습니다.
그들은 일반적으로 두 가지 목표를 염두에 두고 있습니다. 하나는 공모주와 채권을 넘어 투자 포트폴리오를 다각화하는 것이고, 다른 하나에서 얻을 수 있는 것보다 더 나은 수익률을 얻는 것입니다.
바이럴 파텔과 함께 자세히 살펴보겠습니다.
블랙스톤에서 함께 일하는 동료 중 한 명이자 BXPE의 CEO입니다.
좋아요, 그럼 기초부터 시작해 볼까요?
사모펀드란 무엇인가요?
생각만큼 그렇게 복잡하지는 않아요.
대부분의 사람들은 공개 시장에 상장된 기업에 투자하는 것을 생각합니다.
즉, 뉴욕 증권 거래소나 나스닥에서 주식을 사고파는 것입니다.
그 경우에는 사모펀드를 통해 회사의 지분을 사는 것일 뿐입니다.
우리는 회사 전체를 인수하고 있습니다.
하지만 종종 기업이 상장하기 훨씬 이전, 기업의 성장 과정에서 경영진과 협력하여 사업 확장을 돕는 경우가 많습니다.
그리고 나서 어떻게 나가야 할지 알아내는 거죠.
그리고 대개 그 이유는 창업자, 경영진, 기존 소유주가 성장을 위한 방법을 모색하는 데 추가적인 도움을 찾고 있기 때문입니다.
그들은 사업을 더 이상 확장할 수 없다고 판단했고, 이제 다음 단계로 나아가는 데 도움을 줄 파트너를 찾고 있습니다.
그래서 개념은 꽤 간단해 보입니다.
그럼에도 불구하고 이 산업은 지난 몇 년 동안 어느 정도 주목과 관심을 끌어왔습니다.
